The classification, and the thing I most want you to sign off on.

Neither existing partition of stage types fits, which is why this is a third frozenset rather than a reuse:

- `is_grain_and_order_preserving` says output row i came from input row i. `input_data` is in it yet has no input to inherit from, and must declare.
- The signature family says whether a stage adds columns or replaces them. `dedupe` and `explode` are both `ExtendsSignature` — they keep the input's columns — yet both change what one row IS.

So "does this stage's type produce rows of a new kind" is its own fact. It lives here for the same reason the comment above `_GRAIN_AND_ORDER_PRESERVING_TYPES` gives: several layers read it and only core is importable by all of them.

The one I am least sure of is `dedupe`. The argument for it: if the input had five rows per comment because it was scraped five times, the input's rows were sightings and the output's are comments. The argument against: a de-duplicated filing is still a filing, and forcing a word invites the author to coin `deduplicated_filing`. I took the first because the `hate_on_activist_pages` project wrote exactly that distinction into free text ("One row per de-duplicated Meltwater Comment row") — but it is your call.

`python_frame_function` declares because it reshapes freely and only the author knows. It is not in `AUTHORABLE_TYPES`, so the authoring agent never meets it.

The case the type alone gets wrong, and the reason the property exists as well as the function.

An ungrouped aggregate is the ONE stage whose answer depends on its config rather than its type. Its single row is a figure ABOUT the input population, so the sentence #1022 wants reads through it to that population — "the sum of reported expenses **over lobbying filings**". The noun in the clause head is the INPUT's row type, not this stage's.

That is why `declares_its_own_row_type` exists twice: a module function answering about the TYPE (which the prompt catalog and the arch test read) and a property answering about the STAGE, which this overrides. Same shape as `is_grain_and_order_preserving` already had.

New primitive. I looked for an existing one first and rejected what I found.

The repo has the anchor concept in three places — `anchor_read_columns` in `signature.py`, `llm_transform.py:174`, and a comment on `WorkflowStage.inputs` — but all three answer which input's COLUMNS are read. That is a different question: an `enrich` reads columns from both of its inputs and takes its ROWS from the subject alone. Folding them together would have been wrong for `union`, which reads columns from one input shape and takes rows from all of them.

So: one method, `inputs[0]` by default, overridden by `UnionStage` to name every input. That override is what the union check keys off — not `StageType.union` — so a future multi-source type gets the check for free.

The check that makes the whole declaration non-tautological, and the one line in it I would argue about.

Everything else here either refuses a claim a type cannot make or notices an absence. This is the only place where two independently-resolved answers meet and can be caught DISAGREEING — you cannot stack `mill` rows on `filing` rows and call the result one kind of thing.

The line to look at is the `None` filter above. An input that resolved to no row type is dropped before the comparison, so silence never disagrees. The alternative — treating `None` as a third value that conflicts with everything — would fail every workflow already written the moment one stage upstream gained a word, which is the opposite of what you want from a field 895 stored stages leave empty.

Applied to every stage rather than only unions, since for a single-input stage the loop is empty and it costs nothing.

I do not think it can match, and the reason is that `is_grain_and_order_preserving` answers a different question. Laid out per type:

| type | same KIND of row? | same NUMBER? | same ORDER? |
|---|---|---|---|
| python_row_function, llm_transform, human_review_queue, starlark_row_function | yes | yes | yes |
| enrich | yes | yes | yes |
| filter_rows, starlark_filter_rows | yes | **no** | yes |
| sort_rank | yes | yes | **no** |
| union | yes | **no** | **no** |
| expand, explode | **no** | no | no |
| aggregate (grouped) | **no** | no | no |
| python_frame_function | **unknown** | unknown | unknown |
| input_data | creates | — | — |
| report | no rows | — | — |

`is_grain_and_order_preserving` is the top block: 1:1 BY POSITION, which is what the tracer and the eval gate need. Filter, sort and union fall out of it because they change the row SET — but a filtered filing is still a filing, so they change no kinds. That is the mismatch, and it is not removable: one predicate is about positions, the other about meaning.

On `input_data` being in the grain list: I think yes, and for a reason unrelated to row types. Row i of the source is row i of the output, so the positional tracer can align it run to run. Vacuous-looking but load-bearing.

**Explode is not grain preserving — correct**, and it also changes the kind: one row per array element.

**On dedupe, the store falsifies the premise.** Only two distinct dedupe stages have ever been written, and they are one of each kind:

```
one_row_per_grant     keys=[grant_id]            "One row per grant. G-004 was filed in both regions."
dedupe_winning_claim  keys=[uml_id, claim_field] "One claim per mill and field: the one the most
                                                  recently published document made."
```

The first fixes an error — a grant is still a grant. The second is a true regraining: input rows were claims-from-documents, output is one claim per mill per field.

And it could not go through an aggregate. `AggFormula` is `sum, mean, count, count_distinct, min, max, only, list` — `max` returns the extreme VALUE of a column, not the row that carried it. There is no argmax, so "the claim the most recently published document made" is only expressible as `dedupe` with `keep: highest, by: published_date`.

So dedupe has to be able to go either way, which is your other comment exactly. I am keeping it in the declaring set and teaching the distinction in the prompt: dedupe that fixes duplicate rows names the input word again; dedupe that collapses grain names a new one.

Others you were missing: none — `expand` and `python_frame_function` complete the list.

Yes, it can already — through `write_terms`, which replaces the whole vocabulary rather than patching it. Its own tool description tells the agent the idiom: "Store the words this project is written in — the WHOLE vocabulary, all three parts, every time... read_terms first and send that back with your additions rather than sending only what is new."

So adding a row type mid-build is read_terms → append → write_terms. It works, and the refusal for a coined word is not a dead end.

Whether that should be finer-grained CRUD is a real question and I would keep it out of this PR. The replace-whole idiom has one property worth keeping: a word dropped from the payload is a word the project stops using, so retiring vocabulary is expressible. An `add_row_type` tool alongside it would need a `retire_row_type` to stay whole, and then two ways to write the same document. Happy to open an issue if you want it.

Not quite — six types stay in neither set. But the gap is now nameable, which it was not before:

| | |
|---|---|
| **builds new rows** → declares | `aggregate`, `explode`, `expand`, `python_frame_function` |
| **creates rows** → declares | `input_data` |
| **has no rows** → declares | `report` |
| **selects or reorders existing rows** → inherits | `dedupe`, `filter_rows`, `starlark_filter_rows`, `sort_rank`, `union`, `enrich` |
| **maps rows 1:1** → inherits | `python_row_function`, `llm_transform`, `human_review_queue`, `starlark_row_function` |

`is_grain_and_order_preserving` is exactly the last group plus `input_data`. So after your dedupe call the two predicates are adjacent — declaring is "builds", preserving is "maps 1:1" — but complementary they are not: the middle group is neither. A filtered filing is still a filing, so those six change no kinds, and they are not 1:1 by position either, which the tracer depends on.

Removing `input_data` from the preserving set would not close it, and would cost something: row i of the source is row i of the output, so the positional tracer aligns it run to run. It sits in both sets because it has no input — it CREATES rows rather than mapping them, which is a different answer to each question rather than a contradiction.
